name: TempField-HSL Benchmark
description: Thermal issue is of great importance during layout design of heat source components in systems engineering, especially for high functional-density products. Thermal analysis generally needs complex simulation, which leads to an unaffordable computational burden to layout optimization as it iteratively evaluates different schemes. Surrogate modeling is an effective way to alleviate computation complexity. However, temperature field prediction (TFP) with complex heat source layout (HSL) input is an ultra-high dimensional nonlinear regression problem, which brings great difficulty to traditional regression models. The Deep neural network (DNN) regression method is a feasible way for its good approximation performance. However, it faces great challenges in both data preparation for sample diversity and uniformity in the layout space with physical constraints, and proper DNN model selection and training for good generality, which necessitates efforts of both layout designer and DNN experts. To advance this cross-domain research, this paper proposes a DNN based HSL-TFP surrogate modeling task benchmark. With consideration for engineering applicability, sample generation, dataset evaluation, DNN model, and surrogate performance metrics, are thoroughly studied. Experiments are conducted with ten representative state-of-the-art DNN models. Detailed discussion on baseline results is provided and future prospects are analyzed for DNN based HSL-TFP tasks.
evaluation_method: RMSE / L2 error (continuous field prediction metrics)
reputation: A domain-specific benchmark introduced in thermal engineering research; used by researchers working on surrogate modeling and DNN-based temperature-field prediction but not broadly adopted outside that community.
notes: Non-LLM benchmark; high-dimensional input (layout) and output (temperature fields) pose data-economy challenges; results depend strongly on sample diversity and physical-constraint-aware data generation; dataset/model selection sensitivity may cause overfitting or limited generalization.
